extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of poetics/classical drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating tragic drama and epic poetry based on Aristotle's Poetics: what tragedy/epic are, their constituent parts, and the qualities that make them effective. Focuses on plot, character, language, rhythm, and the emotional effects on the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; it uses language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; it is enacted, not narrated; and through pity and fear it effects a catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good tragedy imitates a unified, significant action (not a mere string of episodes), employs suitably elevated language and meter, is performed rather than told, and aims to arouse and purify pity and fear in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (Imitation) as the Poetic Principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and drama are acts of imitation (mimesis) — imitation of actions, characters, and life — using rhythm, language, and harmony, separately or in combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how well a work imitates plausible, necessary human actions rather than merely describing them; the medium (language, rhythm, melody) should serve that imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Constituent Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The six parts of tragedy are: Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), Thought (dianoia), Diction (lexis), Melody/Song (melopoiia), and Spectacle (opsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the axes by which tragedy is judged. Plot is primary, then character and thought; diction and melody concern the verbal/musical expression; spectacle concerns stagecraft and is the least artistic but can have strong impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot (Mythos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot, the arrangement of incidents, is the most important part of tragedy; tragedy is essentially the imitation of an action, so the structure of events is chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the causal and formal arrangement of incidents: a well-ordered plot produces necessary and probable outcomes and is more important than character alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and Completeness of Action
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic plot must be a whole with a beginning, middle, and end; it must be complete (each part necessarily follows and leads to the next) and of a certain magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic sequences without causal unity; ensure each episode contributes to the whole and that the narrative has a coherent causal chain from an identifiable beginning to an inevitable end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude (Scale) Appropriate to the Work
rubrics_metrics.description: The action should be of a certain magnitude — large enough to be serious and complete, though magnitude is not merely length but the scale required by the plot's unity and significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scope and scale so the action feels consequential and complete; too small a scale undermines tragedy, while disproportionate length can dilute unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex vs Simple Plot (Peripeteia and Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either complex (involving reversal of fortune — peripeteia — and/or recognition — anagnorisis) or simple (lacking these). The complex plot with properly combined reversal and recognition is superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex plot that unites reversal and recognition produces the greatest emotional and intellectual effect; simple plots should still preserve unity and necessity but will have less dramatic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of Fortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a change in the action by which the situation turns around to its opposite, e.g., from apparent good to apparent bad fortune (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversal when it follows naturally from the plot's causal structure; avoid contrived twists unmotivated by the preceding action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition/Discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anagnorisis is a change from ignorance to knowledge, especially where the protagonist discovers a critical fact (e.g., identity, motive) that transforms the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition is most effective when it arises from the plot's developments and links causally to reversal, enhancing the audience's experience of necessity and inevitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia / Tragic Error
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's flaw or error (hamartia) — not necessarily moral wickedness — is often the origin of the tragic action; it should be an error in judgment or a mistaken act that leads to suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer flaws or mistakes that are relatable and plausible rather than vice or contrived malevolence; the error should produce pity and fear rather than simple condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity in the Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot must proceed from one another by probability or necessity; the sequence should seem likely or inevitable given what's come before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scenes by whether their outcomes follow plausibly from prior actions; improbable or purely arbitrary events weaken the tragedy's persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (Ethos) — Qualities and Appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Character must be good (or appropriate), consistent, and true to life; characters display qualities fitting the action and are known by their choices and speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A protagonist should be neither wholly good nor wholly bad (so as to elicit pity/fear); characters must act consistent with their established nature and social role, and their speeches should reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (Dianoia) — Reasoning and Themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty by which meanings, themes, arguments, and the characters' reasoning are expressed in speech and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the plausibility and persuasiveness of the themes and arguments expressed; thought is shown in what characters decide and assert, and it should cohere with the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction/Style (Lexis) and Use of Metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction concerns the expression of the arguments and feelings in appropriate language and choice of words, including the effective use of metaphor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language should be clear, elevated as appropriate to the serious subject, and employ apt metaphors; the choice of words influences the perceived character and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody/Song (Melopoiia) — Choral Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody refers to the musical element of tragedy (choral song), an embellishment that adds to the emotional effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use choral and musical components to intensify mood and underscore themes, while ensuring they integrate with the plot and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) — Visual Stagecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle concerns the visual aspects of the performance — scenery, costumes, effects — and while powerful, it is the least artistic element with respect to poetry itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on spectacle to enhance impact but not as a substitute for strong plot and character; great spectacle cannot compensate for poor poetic structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enacted Representation vs. Narrative Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should present actions through enacted scenes (drama), not through narrative recounting; showing is superior to telling for poetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer scenes that enact turning points and discoveries rather than long narrated summaries; the audience should witness causation rather than be told it afterward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: Effect on the Audience (Pity and Fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal aim of tragedy is to arouse pity and fear and thereby achieve a catharsis (purging or purification) of such emotions in the spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the degree to which the work reliably evokes pity and fear through its plot and characters, leading to a satisfying emotional resolution rather than mere sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs. Tragedy: Comparative Criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and tragedy share many qualities (imitation of action), but differ in means and magnitude: epic uses narrative meter (e.g., hexameter), is longer, and can include multiple actions; tragedy is enacted, uses meter appropriate to the stage, and aims for unified action and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare works by how they handle unity, scale, medium (narrative vs enactment), and the degree of concentrated emotional effect; longer scope in epic allows for variety but can sacrifice unity.
